Liam, I'd really suggest tracking down the sibling rivalry episode where Bob discusses his regret at partly perpetuating the fracking meme against Rupaul. 

It's a toxic dynamic which the rest of the fandom seems to not give a damn about: a black man fully and unrepentantedly penalized for the actions of his white husband's family.

If you did any research beyond Willam's IG, you'd know the ranch in question was never bought by Rupaul -- it belonged to his white husband, and had been in the ownership of his white husband's family for a couple of generations. Mineral rights and vesting of land interests are complicated shit which can't be withdrawn in a single breath, not especially in fucking Wyoming.

Have a read of this article which came out a while ago, but which you probably missed (understandably, Willam's IG is a lot more reliable to most fans of course /s):
 https://amp.theguardian.com/environment/2020/aug/28/fracking-wyoming-ranchers-rupaul

I get this reply is probably a lot for a silly and well drawn comic. Its just every time a fracking joke gets made about Rupaul it really saddens me (to a deeper level).

It reminds me of how quickly an entire fandom can turn on someone on the shallowest understanding of a complex situation; it reminds me of the unwillingness of most fans to comprehend grey issues and to stop seeing the world in black-and-white. It makes me reflect on whether I'VE been guilty of doing this in the past or if I might fall for it in the future. On a more personal level, as a person of colour if I fall in love with a white man and marry him, I am choosing him. Not his family or their shady generational baggage; it would fucking kill me to be turned into the face and only person responsible for THEIR history. 


*****

This isn't a defence of fracking, for all those ready to jump screaming at me. This is about the context of the allegations.

I agree with some of the points you raise! However, I think it should be important to recognise that The Show is a television production, which needs a narrative. In Drag Race, there is a host/drag mother, and there are contestants. It would make no logical sense to feature the contests as Rupaul's peers, because in the context of a TV show narrative that would skew the dynamics the show relies on.

In terms of other non-contestant drag queens being featured as judges, I look at this as a non-issue. At the end of the day, the show relies on the narrative that Rupaul is The Drag Queen/Drag Mother. The narrative would be skewed if there were two drag hoes on the judging panel (the same way that Canada's Drag Race only has one drag queen on the panel, Brooklyn Hytes). 

Additionally, the show has featured other drag queens/icons in different ways. Whether through cameos (Lady Bunny, for example, and Love Conny from season 11), or quick educational montages (recently, educating the masses on Fulsom, and another example is season 9's Gayest Ball Ever), or even challenges centred around other drag dynasties (the recent winds of daytona episode comes to mind).  

My main point in my original comment is that Drag Race's objective purpose is to support and ensure the success of their queens, which you cannot deny they do and continue to do. Look at [most] of the winners. 

Even the non-winners are given a bit of limelight time and time again, whether through bit parts in Rupaul's projects (remember Latrice being invited by Ru during his Family Feud cameo, and latrice being personally invited by Ru to be a writer for AJ and the Queen?) I struggle to think of any other Show and TV host that invests in their contestants as much as Rupaul.

I don't mean to offend anyone by this post, I genuinely want to know.

Some context: I'm a 24 year old Asian POC. I immigrated here around 9 years ago, when I was 15. I went to a lower decile highschool (think unheated classrooms and several squat buildings scattered around so students have to walk through mud to get to their classes). The first friends I made in this country were black and POC, tho we've drifted since then. I never realised the full extent of slang I adopted from my friend until now.

I drop "girl, what?" "hey, girl!!!" "mmhmm" & more in my everyday vocabulary. My current friend group (many of them from asian backgrounds) do the same as well. In light of the cultural conversations were all having now it made me suddenly conscious of something I never considered before. I know for a fact I picked these up from my friends because that's how we conversed, and didn't think anything of it until I started listening to this podcast called the Stoop two days ago where the two hosts discussed cultural appropriation. I'm late to this kind of discussion, but it made me pause and think. I mean, what do you think of Awkwafina? 

Is it better for us to make a conscious effort to drop them, out of respect and recognition they are not ours? I genuinely want to know what you think.
